title: A strategy to eliminate carbon deposition on a copper electrode in order to enhance its stability in CO2RR catalysis by introducing crystal defects
abstract: Cu is the only electrocatalyst that converts CO2 into appreciable quantities of hydrocarbons. However, it usually suffers from poor catalytic stability. In this work we propose a strategy of introducing crystal defects to change the reaction pathway and avoid accumulation of carbon on the Cu electrode surface, thus preventing its deactivation. Our experimental results show that carbon accumulation vanished and catalytic stability improved after crystal defects had been introduced into nano Cu electrodes. The correlation between the two rules: (1) crystal defects facilitate C2H4 formation while suppress CH4 generation; (2) crystal defects improve catalytic stability, reveals that the C2H4 formation pathway bypasses the carbon deposition associated with CH4 formation and results in stable catalytic performance. In particular, the Cu catalyst prepared according to this principle performed with good stability for 6 h almost without any change in Faradaic efficiency. This work may provide a new approach to stable CO2RR catalysis by managing the reaction pathway.

A B S T R A C T
Cu is the only electrocatalyst that converts CO2 into appreciable quantities of hydrocarbons. However, it usually suffers from poor catalytic stability. In this work we propose a strategy of introducing crystal defects to change the reaction pathway and avoid accumulation of carbon on the Cu electrode surface, thus preventing its deactivation. Our experimental results show that carbon accumulation vanished and catalytic stability improved after crystal defects had been introduced into nano Cu electrodes. The correlation between the two rules: (1) crystal defects facilitate C2H4 formation while suppress CH4 generation; (2) crystal defects improve catalytic stability, reveals that the C2H4 formation pathway bypasses the carbon deposition associated with CH4 formation and results in stable catalytic performance. In particular, the Cu catalyst prepared according to this principle performed with good stability for 6 h almost without any change in Faradaic efficiency. This work may provide a new approach to stable CO2RR catalysis by managing the reaction pathway.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere is increasing year by year and the resulting greenhouse effects have attracted global attention [1,2]. In recent years, the concept of carbon neutrality has been gradually accepted, in which converting CO2 to useful chemicals or fuels play an important role. A number of commodity chemicals, including carbon monoxide, formic acid, methane, ethylene and ethanol, have been successfully synthesized through electrochemical reduction of CO2 by various catalysts [3]. Among these catalysts, Cu has excellent performance in converting CO2 to hydrocarbons [4,5], and has been widely studied for this reason.
A large number of studies have aimed to design a high-performance Cu catalyst, but these have mainly focused on improving product selectivity [6–8]. By contrast, the deactivation of the Cu electrode has not received as much attention as it deserves [9–11]. The reason for the catalytic instability of Cu electrodes is still controversial. Recent studies have suggested that deactivation of Cu electrodes originates with the deposition of carbon species during the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) [12]. For this reason, Weng et al. utilized foreign atoms (Pd, Rh) to induce the restructuring of the Cu surface, which constantly refreshed the catalyst surface and thus maintained its catalytic properties for CO2
reduction [12]. This method provided an approach to avoid the effects of deposited carbon by burying it beneath the surface, but does not eliminate the deposited carbon. This means that the deactivation will occur again when the surface refresh stops as the Pd or Rh lose their affinity to the surface Cu atoms due to the increased Cu thickness. To date, no studies have reported an approach which eliminates carbon deposition during the CO2RR.
As previously reported, the carbon formation pathway is correlated with the products of CO2RR [13]. Some researchers have suggested that a carbon intermediate could be formed during the CH4 formation pathway [14,15]. Switching the CH4 formation pathway to a parallel pathway to generate C2H4 may avoid carbon formation and accumulation. It has been reported that the important step in C2H4 formation, CO-CO dimerization, occurs more easily on Cu atoms at crystal defects due to the stronger adsorption towards CO intermediates [16]. Therefore, guiding the CO2RR pathway by introducing defects into a Cu electrode opens the possibility of preventing deactivation. In this work, we present the pathway-guided tactics of avoiding carbon formation and accumulation on a Cu electrode in order to obtain good catalytic stability.

sections.heading: 2. Experiments
sections.text:
The Cu nanocatalyst was prepared as follows. 1 mL Cu(NO3)2 (5 mM) was pipetted into 20 mL concentrated NaOH solution (15 M) in a glass flask under magnetic stirring at a rate of 250 rpm for 5 min. Then 0.1 mL ethylenediamine (EDA) was added to the above solution. The solution was heated to 70 °C, and 10.5 μL N2H4 solution (35 wt% in water) was added to the solution with magnetic stirring at a rate of 500 rpm. The temperature and stirring were maintained for another 60 min, then the solid and liquid were separated using a piece of filter membrane (0.45 μm) and a vacuum filtration setup. Plenty of purified water was used to wash the reddish-brown solid left on the filter membrane. The reddish-brown solid was collected and followed by vacuum drying at 60 °C for 8 h. This was followed by an annealing treatment. The as-prepared copper nanoneedles (CuNNs) were placed in a tube furnace under high purity Ar flowing at a rate of 30 mL/min (the resulting material is referred to as annealed Cu). The annealing
temperature was set at 500 °C for 3 h. For the oxidation treatment, the Ar was replaced by air with other procedures remaining the same (resulting material denoted as OT-Cu). The chemicals were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.
X-ray diffraction spectra were obtained with a Rigaku TRIII. SEM images were acquired with a JEOL IT300 Scanning Electron Microscope. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) was performed using a JEM-2100F (JEOL Ltd., Japan). XPS measurements were performed with an Escalab 250Xi (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using a monochromatic 1486.7 eV Al Kα X-ray source. Raman spectroscopy (Renishaw inVia) with a 532-nm pump laser was used to detect the carbon species on the Cu electrodes before and after electrolysis. For the Raman tests, the catalysts were dispensed on a 1 × 1 cm clean Cu foil instead of a glassy carbon substrate without adding Nafion as binder, to make it easier to transfer samples and to avoid the interference of external carbon sources.
All electrochemical tests were performed using a three-electrode cell
on an electrochemical work station (CHI 760D, Shanghai, China). A platinum plate 2 × 2 cm in size was employed as the counter electrode and Ag/AgCl (in 3 M KCl solution) soaked in a Luggin capillary was used as the reference electrode. The cathode compartment and anode compartment were separated by a piece of proton exchange membrane (Nafion 117, DuPont) to prevent re-oxidation of the products. The cathode compartment was gas-tight and connected with a gas chromatograph (GC, Shimadzu GC2010). 0.5 M KHCO3 solution was used as the electrolyte. The electrolysis cell had a volume of 100 mL in each compartment, and 60 mL electrolyte was used for each electrolysis test. Before the CO2 electroreduction tests, the electrolyte was bubbled with high purity CO2 (30 mL/min) for at least 30 min. The Cu electrodes were prepared by the following procedures: 5 mg powder (for CuNNs and annealed CuNNs), or 7.5 mg (for CuO NNs) and 40 μL Nafion solution (5 wt%) were dispersed in 500 μL DI water and 500 μL absolute ethyl alcohol by sonication to form a homogenous ink. 50 μL of the dispersed ink was then dropped on the glassy carbon electrode (1 × 1 cm).
During the chronoamperometric electrolysis, the gaseous products (H2, CO and hydrocarbons) were detected by gas chromatography (GC 2010, Shimadzu; SH-Rt-Q-BOND PLOT column) equipped with a Barrier Discharge Ionization Detector (BID, Shimadzu). After a 3 h electrolysis, the electrolyte was sampled and analysed by ion chromatography (IC, Metrohm 883 Basic IC plus) and headspace gas chromatography (GC 2010, Shimadzu; InertCap FFAP capillary column).

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
To test the predictions experimentally, we prepared a couple of Cu electrodes with different levels of crystal defects but with same nanoneedle morphology. First, we prepared Cu nanoneedles (CuNNs, Fig. S1) with a 1D structure due to their easy formation of crystal defects [17–19]. These CuNNs showed initial signs of catalytic stability reflected by the stable current density (Fig. S2). Based on this platform, we further managed the amount of crystal defects in the CuNNs by annealing in an Ar atmosphere and using oxidation/reduction processes to eliminate and increase the level of defects, respectively (illustrated in Fig. 1a). Fig. 1(b,c) shows the SEM and TEM images of the CuNNs before and after annealing or oxidation/reduction, demonstrating the consistency in morphology with 100–200 nm diameter and 3–5 μm length. The XRD patterns in Fig. 1d indicate that the treatment does not change the phase of the material (Cu0, JPCDS 85-1362), but the grain sizes varied from 48.6 to 34.3 nm (Fig. S3). A previous study has shown that a smaller grain size is associated with more defects [20]. That means that the concentration of defects may be different due to grain size changes [21,22]. Notably, the Cu2p of XPS in Fig. 1e shows that the OT-CuNNs sample was vulnerable to oxidation, and the O1s spectrum demonstrated that the adsorbed O species (Oad at 531.2 eV) ratio increased in the following order: annealed CuNNs < CuNNs < OTCuNNs. Previous studies have shown that crystal defects such as grain boundaries can act as nucleation sites to adsorb O species (Oad) to accelerate the oxidation of the Cu surface [23]. Therefore, the increasing concentration of defects could explain the increased ratio of Oad in annealed Cu, CuNNs and OT-CuNNs.
To test the catalytic behaviour of the CuNNs towards CO2 reduction, the as-prepared Cu electrodes were tested electrochemically. The electrochemical characterization was carried out by potentiostatic electrolysis at a potential of −1.4 V (versus Ag/AgCl) in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution electrolyte. The gaseous products were measured by online gas chromatography at intervals of 30 min during the electrolysis, while the liquid products could only be identified when the electrolysis was complete (Fig. S4). Therefore, the investigation of catalytic stability will be based on the gaseous products. During the electrolysis process, an obvious deactivation of the annealed CuNNs can
be seen in Fig. 2a. The Faradaic efficiency for H2 obviously increased over time, while the Faradaic efficiencies for CO, CH4 and C2H4 fluctuated. By contrast, very stable Faradaic efficiencies for gaseous products were achieved on CuNNs and OT-CuNNs electrodes over the whole electrolysis process (Fig. 2(b,c)). In particular, the Faradaic efficiency of C2H4 increased to 15% on the CuNNs electrode and 52% on OT-CuNNs respectively, which is much higher than on the annealed CuNNs. The Faradaic efficiency of CH4 decreased from 7% for annealed CuNNs to 4% and 1.8% for CuNNs and OT-CuNNs, respectively. The change in Faradaic efficiency for CO on the Cu electrode was consistent with that of CH4. The i-t curves also revealed that the catalytic behaviour on the annealed CuNNs is not stable, as also shown by the exchange current density decaying from 10 to 4.5 mA/cm2 within 3 h. However, the CuNNs and OT-CuNNs performed in a stable way during the long-term electrolysis. Further, we investigated the relationship between the density of crystal defects and catalytic stability by establishing a correlation between the standard deviation of the products' Faradaic efficiency versus electrolysis time. In this representation, the higher the value of the standard deviation, the worse the stability performance. This demonstrated that the catalytic stability of Cu electrodes was correlated positively with the density of crystal defects (Fig. 2e), revealing the key role of crystal defects in stabilizing catalytic activity and selectivity, and endorsing our proposed strategy to obtain a stable Cu electrode.
In previous studies, deactivation of the Cu electrode was explained by poisoning due to carbon or organic products. This was deduced from the C signal in the XPS analysis [24]. However, the XPS results could not distinguish where the carbon really came from (bicarbonate electrolyte or internal standard). Raman spectroscopy is a sensitive method of analyzing carbon, especially graphitized carbon, and so this technique was employed to detect the carbon signal on the Cu surface [25] (Fig. 2f). Peaks at 1347 and 1596 cm−1, which are consistent with the characteristic Raman signal of graphitized carbon [26], showed an obvious increase on the annealed CuNNs after 3 h electrolysis. However, no obvious increase in the carbon signal was observed on the OTCuNNs after 3 h electrolysis. It should be noted that the typical graphitized carbon signal shows that the carbon species is derived from the reduction process rather than carbon contamination. As previously reported, the carbon accumulation on Cu may subsequently contribute to increased H2 evolution and decreased CO2RR performance [15], which is consistent with the trend of Faradaic efficiency changes on the annealed CuNNs (Fig. 2a). Taking these together, it was speculated that carbon accumulation on the surface of the annealed CuNNs lead to a deterioration in catalytic stability.
The variation in Faradaic efficiency between the various Cu electrodes revealed that the different treatment of CuNNs leads to a different distribution of products, especially C2H4. Notably, an obvious improvement in Faradaic efficiency for C2H4 was obtained when the amount of crystal defects in the Cu electrode increased. However, in contrast, the Faradaic efficiency for CH4 decreased. We analysed the electrochemically active area (ECSA, derived from Fig. S5 and Table S1) normalized current for C2H4 and CH4 on the different Cu electrodes studied (Fig. 3a). The increased jC2H4 means higher turnover frequency (TOF) for C2H4, which is consistent with the variation of crystal defects in the annealed CuNNs, CuNNs and OT-CuNNs, while the situation is just the opposite for CH4. Therefore, the defects provide specific selectivity towards C2H4 formation, while suppressing the formation of CH4. To investigate the reason for this phenomenon, a CO electroadsorption test was performed because CO is a very important intermediate in CO2RR. It is known that the CO2RR pathway is sensitive to the CO adsorption state. It has been suggested that the surface coverage of CO* determines the distribution of products [27,28]. Recent theoretical studies have shown that the CO dimerization step is rate-determining, and higher coverage of CO is beneficial for CO dimerization
leading to C2H4 formation [29,30]. The CO electroadsorption tests (Fig. 3b) show that the OT-CuNNs have a more positive potential (−1.41 V v.s −1.48 V) to adsorb CO and larger integral area in the voltammetry curves compared to untreated CuNNs, though the ECSA of the OT-CuNNs is smaller. This indicates that crystal defects are beneficial for CO adsorption, which ensures sufficient CO for the dimerization process to form C2H4 [16]. This proposition is also supported by the work of Boon Siang Yeo, which demonstrated that the adsorption of intermediates, including CO, is significantly enhanced on Cu2O-derived Cu with smaller crystallite sizes (actually, more defects such as grain boundaries and particle junctions) to form C2+ products [20]. For this reason, the OT-CuNNs, which have more crystal defects, performed better in converting the CO intermediate into C2H4 in the CO2RR process.
Taking these results together, a rule could be formulated that the preferred C2H4 formation on crystal-defect-rich Cu electrodes contributes to better catalytic stability. Cu electrodes with fewer defects (annealed CuNNs) have low C2H4 selectivity but higher CH4 conversion ability and are prone to catalytic instability. It is inferred that the carbon deposition causing deactivation can be ascribed to the CH4 formation pathway. To verify the speculation regarding instability on Cu electrodes, Cu foil, which is considered as a good platform for generating CH4, was used. As expected, the Cu foil deactivates rapidly in the first hour (Fig. S6). Meanwhile, the surface of the Cu foil was also covered with detectable amounts of carbon after a 3 h electrolysis, as revealed by the Raman spectra (Fig. S7). This supports the assertion that the CH4 pathway results in carbon deposition, which is also in good agreement with the DFT predicted pathway for CH4 formation [13].
At this point, the reason for the difference in catalytic stability is clear. The conversion pathway of CO determines whether the electrode surface is poisoned by carbon deposition or not. According to previous DFT studies by Jens K. Nørskov, CO is reduced to form CHO or COH through formation of a CeH or OeH bond [31]. Recently, Nie et al.
reported that the COH path is favoured over the CHO path by a selectivity factor of around 2000 at 300 K, and the COH pathway to form CH4 will follow: COH → C → CH → CH2 → CH3 → CH4 [13]. At the same time, a CO dimerization process to form C2H4 as discussed above is also possible. Therefore, two pathways may coexist in the CO2RR (depicted in Fig. S8): the CO dimer pathway towards C2H4 and the COH pathway towards CH4. The opposite trend of jC2H4 and jCH4 on different Cu electrodes implies that the two pathways are competitive due to the shared CO intermediate. Because the crystal defects in the Cu electrode could enhance CO adsorption, CuNNs with more crystal defects tend to take the CO dimer pathway to form C2H4 and suppress the COH pathway to produce CH4. This behaviour reduces carbon formation in the CO2RR process, thus prolonging the durability of the electrode (Fig. 3c-I). With fewer crystal defects, Cu electrodes favouring CH4 formation tend to be unstable in CO2RR due to the deposition of carbon during the CH4 formation process, which is in good agreement with the character of the COH pathway to form a C intermediate. As the catalysis continues, the active sites for CO2RR are covered by deposited carbon, leading to deactivation and enhanced hydrogen evolution (Fig. 3c-II).
Previous work has reported that catalytic performance in the CO2RR may be greatly influenced by nanoneedle morphology [32]. To test whether this specific morphology accounts for the catalytic stability, in another experiment we used Cu nanoparticles (CuNPs) and OT-CuNPs for comparison (Fig. S9). The similar catalytic stability and Faradaic efficiencies of the OT-CuNNs and OT-CuNPs strongly suggests that the stability was not due to the sharp-tip enhancement effect but rather dominated by crystal defects. Meanwhile, this experiment demonstrated the generality of the low carbon accumulation pathway in retaining the catalytic stability of Cu electrodes in CO2RR (Table S2). This strategy may also give us some indications regarding the stable conversion of CO2 mainly towards C2+ products and suggests a general principle for the design of stable electrodes in CO2RR catalysis.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text: We present a strategy to induce a CO2RR pathway that could avoid accumulation of carbon species on a Cu electrode to maintain catalytic stability. This strategy could easily be realized by introducing crystal defects to guide the CO2RR pathway towards the formation of C2H4. This provides researchers with a new approach to achieving stable CO2RR catalysis by managing the reaction pathway.
